claim: Galectin-9 binds directly to IgM-BCR and CD45.
source: Galectin-9 (Gal9) is a soluble, bivalent glycan-binding protein that binds directly to IgM-BCR and CD45 (Cao et al., 2018; Giovannone et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Cao et al., 2018; Giovannone et al., 2018)

claim: Binding of Gal9 alters the organization of the BCR, enhancing interactions with inhibitory co-receptors CD45 and CD22.
source: Binding of Gal9 alters the organization of the BCR, enhancing interactions with inhibitory co-receptors CD45 and CD22, thereby reducing BCR signal transduction (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Cao et al., 2018)

claim: Loss of Gal9 in mice results in spontaneous autoimmunity with age, marked by splenomegaly, spontaneous germinal center formation, autoantibody production, and nephritis.
source: Here, we demonstrate that loss of Gal9 in mice results in a breakdown of peripheral tolerance and leads to spontaneous autoimmunity with age, marked by splenomegaly, spontaneous germinal center formation, autoantibody production, and nephritis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3)

claim: Gal9 regulates the threshold of follicular B cell activation.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that Gal9 regulates the threshold of follicular B cell activation, and loss of this regulatory network permits activation to low-affinity and low-density antigens.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1 and 2)

claim: Loss of Gal9 permits B cell activation to low-affinity and low-density antigens.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that Gal9 regulates the threshold of follicular B cell activation, and loss of this regulatory network permits activation to low-affinity and low-density antigens.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1 and 2)

claim: There is an expansion in the B-1a compartment in the absence of Gal9.
source: Additionally, we observe an expansion in the B-1a compartment in the absence of Gal9 and demonstrate that these B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, are more sensitive to BCR and distinct toll-like receptor (TLR) stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 4)

claim: B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, are more sensitive to BCR and distinct TLR stimuli in the absence of Gal9.
source: Additionally, we observe an expansion in the B-1a compartment in the absence of Gal9 and demonstrate that these B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, are more sensitive to BCR and distinct toll-like receptor (TLR) stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 5 and 6)

claim: Gal9 directly regulates BCR and distinct TLRs by binding to IgM-BCR and CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells.
source: We identify that Gal9 directly regulates BCR and distinct TLRs by binding to IgM-BCR and CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells as well as TLR4 and the regulatory molecule CD180, dampening signal transduction by altering their nano-scale co-distribution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 5 and 6)

claim: Gal9 binds to TLR4 and CD180 on B-1a cells.
source: We identify that Gal9 directly regulates BCR and distinct TLRs by binding to IgM-BCR and CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells as well as TLR4 and the regulatory molecule CD180, dampening signal transduction by altering their nano-scale co-distribution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 6)

claim: Gal9 dampens signal transduction by altering the nano-scale co-distribution of receptors and regulatory molecules.
source: We identify that Gal9 directly regulates BCR and distinct TLRs by binding to IgM-BCR and CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells as well as TLR4 and the regulatory molecule CD180, dampening signal transduction by altering their nano-scale co-distribution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 5 and 6)

claim: Enhanced activation of B-1a cells in the absence of Gal9 exacerbates autoimmunity by facilitating transfer of autoantigens to secondary lymphoid organs.
source: We demonstrate that enhanced activation of B-1a cells in the absence of Gal9 is detrimental and exacerbates autoimmunity by facilitating transfer of autoantigens to secondary lymphoid organs where they drive autoimmune responses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 7)

claim: BCR signal strength upon antigen binding is defined by co-receptors that fine-tune signal transduction.
source: BCR signal strength upon antigen binding is defined by a host of co-receptors that fine-tune and co-ordinate signal transduction.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about BCR signaling

claim: Increased BCR signal strength leads to productive B cell activation when antigen affinity or concentrations are limiting.
source: Increased signal strength leads to productive B cell activation when antigen affinity or concentrations are limiting (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017)

claim: BCR co-receptors modulate BCR signaling and define the threshold of antigen required for B cell activation.
source: Therefore, BCR co-receptors modulate BCR signaling and define the threshold of antigen required for B cell activation (Tedder et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Tedder et al., 1997)

claim: BCR signaling is enhanced at limiting antigen concentrations in Gal9KO B cells compared to WT B cells.
source: In the absence of Gal9, however, BCR signaling is enhanced at limiting antigen concentrations compared to WT B cells (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: IgM internalization is increased in Gal9KO B cells compared to WT B cells in the context of reduced antigen concentrations.
source: Notably, in the context of reduced antigen concentrations, IgM internalization is increased in Gal9KO compared to WT B cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Gal9KO B cells internalize IgM at a faster rate than WT B cells.
source: To quantify the rate of IgM internalization, we plotted the rate of change (k) of the fitted decay curve, which revealed Gal9KO B cells internalize IgM at a faster rate than WT B cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Increased BCR signaling in Gal9-deficient B cells leads to an increase in internalization of IgM-BCR.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that increased BCR signaling in Gal9-deficient B cells leads to an increase in internalization of IgM-BCR.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: BCR signal transduction to low-dose stimuli is enhanced in the absence of Gal9.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, BCR signal transduction to low-dose stimuli, as measured by the gMFI of the GFP reporter, is enhanced in the absence of Gal9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The extent of BCR signaling correlates with the rate of BCR internalization.
source: Furthermore, the extent of BCR signaling (gMFI of GFP) correlates with the rate of BCR internalization over the same interval (k, over 20 min) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Gal9 regulates BCR internalization through modulating BCR signal strength.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates BCR internalization through modulating BCR signal strength.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In the absence of Gal9, B cells respond to lower concentrations of antigen as measured by CD86 upregulation.
source: Following 16 hr of stimulation we see increased B cell activation proportional to increasing concentration of anti-IgM; however, in the absence of Gal9 B cells respond to lower concentrations of antigen (Figure 1F), quantified by the decreased EC50 value (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G

claim: Gal9 restrains B cell activation when antigen concentrations are limiting.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 restrains B cell activation when antigen concentrations are limiting.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Many myeloid cell populations have high levels of intracellular and extracellular Gal9 expression.
source: Interestingly, we see high levels of intracellular and extracellular Gal9 expression from many myeloid cell populations, with little detectable Gal9 from the T cell compartment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: T cells have little detectable Gal9 expression.
source: Interestingly, we see high levels of intracellular and extracellular Gal9 expression from many myeloid cell populations, with little detectable Gal9 from the T cell compartment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: B cells have the highest Gal9 expression relative to abundance within the spleen when factoring in subset abundance.
source: We see that when we factor in subset abundance, B cells appear to have the highest Gal9 expression relative to abundance within the spleen.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Both B cell-derived and macrophage-derived Gal9 contribute to extrinsic sources of Gal9 within the splenic environment.
source: Additionally, Gal9 expression was only partially restored when Gal9KO B cells were transferred into macrophage depleted or B cell-deficient hosts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F), demonstrating that both B cell-derived and macrophage-derived Gal9 contribute to extrinsic sources of Gal9 within the splenic environment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F

claim: Macrophage populations and B cells act as a source of Gal9 within the spleen.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that macrophage populations and B cells act as a source of Gal9 within the spleen and that these sources of extrinsic Gal9 are sufficient to alter the threshold of B cell activation.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Extrinsic sources of Gal9 are sufficient to alter the threshold of B cell activation.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that macrophage populations and B cells act as a source of Gal9 within the spleen and that these sources of extrinsic Gal9 are sufficient to alter the threshold of B cell activation.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: MD4 B cells express an IgM-BCR specific for hen egg lysozyme (HEL) with Ka = 4.5 × 10^10 M^-1.
source: In this model, B cells express an IgM-BCR specific for model antigen hen egg lysozyme, HEL (HyHEL10, Ka = 4.5 × 1010 M−1).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the MD4 transgenic system

claim: MD4 B cells bind to Bobwhite Quail lysozyme (QEL) with reduced affinity (Ka = 3 × 10^8 M^-1).
source: MD4 B cells bind to lysozymes from other avian species with reduced affinity, such as Bobwhite Quail (QEL, Ka = 3 × 108 M−1) and Duck (DEL, Ka = 1.7 × 107 M−1) (Lavoie et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Lavoie et al., 1992)

claim: MD4 B cells bind to Duck lysozyme (DEL) with reduced affinity (Ka = 1.7 × 10^7 M^-1).
source: MD4 B cells bind to lysozymes from other avian species with reduced affinity, such as Bobwhite Quail (QEL, Ka = 3 × 108 M−1) and Duck (DEL, Ka = 1.7 × 107 M−1) (Lavoie et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Lavoie et al., 1992)

claim: Gal9KO B cells spread more and accumulate more antigen in response to low-affinity antigens compared to WT B cells on lipid bilayers.
source: Gal9KO B cells appear to spread more and accumulate more antigen in response to lower affinity antigens compared to WT B cells. To quantify this, we measured the contact area and total amount of antigen accumulated (Figure 2B,C). Indeed, Gal9KO B cells spread more and accumulate more antigen in response to low-affinity antigens presented on lipid bilayers compared to WT B cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: The B cell spreading response and the amount of antigen accumulated is regulated by BCR signaling.
source: It is well established that the B cell spreading response, and thus the amount of antigen accumulated is regulated by BCR signaling (Fleire et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Fleire et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2008)

claim: In the absence of Gal9, BCR signaling is increased in response to low-affinity and low-density membrane-bound antigens compared to WT B cells.
source: In the absence of Gal9, BCR signaling is increased in response to low-affinity and low-density membrane-bound antigens compared to WT B cells (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: Loss of Gal9 leads to increased upregulation of CD86 in response to lower concentrations of lysozyme antigens.
source: In the absence of Gal9, upregulation of CD86 is increased in response to lower concentrations of antigen in all three affinities of lysozyme (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: In the absence of Gal9, B cells internalize IgM at a faster rate in response to low-affinity antigens compared to WT B cells.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of Gal9, B cells internalize IgM at a faster rate in response to low-affinity antigens compared to WT B cells (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Gal9KO B cells internalize a greater amount of IgM and antigen when stimulated with low-affinity antigens compared to WT B cells.
source: This results in a greater amount of IgM and antigen internalized in Gal9KO B cells when stimulated with low-affinity antigens (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Gal9 regulates B cell responsiveness to low-affinity and low-density antigens.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates B cell responsiveness to low-affinity and low-density antigens.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 2

claim: Aged Gal9KO mice have enlarged spleens.
source: We find that aged Gal9KO mice have enlarged spleens (Figure 3A), with detectable germinal center (GC) B cells in the absence of immunization, suggesting they are driven toward autoantigens (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Aged Gal9KO mice have detectable germinal center B cells in the absence of immunization.
source: We find that aged Gal9KO mice have enlarged spleens (Figure 3A), with detectable germinal center (GC) B cells in the absence of immunization, suggesting they are driven toward autoantigens (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: Gal9KO mice have enhanced antibody secreting cell (ASC) development in the spleen compared with WT littermate controls.
source: Furthermore, we see enhanced antibody secreting cell (ASC; defined as FSChi, surface IgMneg, and CD138hi expressing cells) (Pracht et al., 2017) development in the spleen of Gal9KO mice compared with WT littermate controls (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: There is a clear skewing toward B220-negative long-lived ASCs in the absence of Gal9.
source: Further characterization of the ASC compartment revealed a clear skewing toward B220-negative long-lived ASCs in the absence of Gal9 (Pracht et al., 2017; Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: There is an increased frequency of B220- ASCs in the bone marrow in the absence of Gal9.
source: Consistent with this, we observe increased frequency of B220- ASCs in the bone marrow the absence of Gal9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Aged Gal9KO mice have increased autoreactivity to HEp-2 cells with circulating IgG antibodies that are largely nuclear-reactive and circulating IgM that are largely cytoplasmically reactive.
source: We see increased autoreactivity to HEp-2 cells with serum from Gal9KO mice compared to WT controls, having circulating IgG antibodies that are largely nuclear-reactive and circulating IgM that are largely cytoplasmically reactive (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G,H

claim: Antigen-specific anti-dsDNA and anti-GME autoantibodies are increased in Gal9KO mice.
source: Furthermore, antigen-specific anti-dsDNA and anti-GME (glomerular membrane extract) autoantibodies are increased in Gal9KO mice (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I,J

claim: Aged Gal9KO mice have an increase in circulating immune complexes in the serum.
source: We observe an increase in circulating ICs in the serum (Figure 3K) as well as increased proteinuria (Figure 3L), indicative of nephritis, in aged Gal9KO mice compared to WT controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K

claim: Aged Gal9KO mice have increased proteinuria, indicative of nephritis.
source: We observe an increase in circulating ICs in the serum (Figure 3K) as well as increased proteinuria (Figure 3L), indicative of nephritis, in aged Gal9KO mice compared to WT controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L

claim: Gal9KO mice develop spontaneous autoimmunity with age.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that Gal9KO mice develop spontaneous autoimmunity with age.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: Aged Gal9KO mice have an increase in Tfh cell frequency.
source: We see that aged Gal9KO mice have an increase in Tfh cell frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), mirroring the increase in GC B cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: The ratio of regulatory Tfr cells to Tfh cells is similar in both WT and Gal9KO mice.
source: Additionally, we observe a similar increase in the frequency of FoxP3+ Tfr cells in the spleen of Gal9KO mice; however, the ratio of regulatory Tfr cells to Tfh cells is similar in both WT and Gal9KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G

claim: Loss of Gal9 does not lead to spontaneous autoimmunity through impaired generation of regulatory Tfh cells.
source: These data suggest that loss of Gal9 does not lead to spontaneous autoimmunity through impaired generation of regulatory Tfh cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: A distinct population of cells in the spleen of Gal9KO MD4/ML5 mice retain high levels of surface IgM.
source: We observed a distinct population of cells in the spleen of Gal9KO MD4/ML5 mice that retain high levels of surface IgM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H,I

claim: The IgM-high population in Gal9KO MD4/ML5 mice induces robust signaling compared to both anergic WT cells and IgM-low anergic-like cells in Gal9KO mice.
source: Furthermore, following IgM stimulation, this population induces robust signaling compared to both anergic WT cells and IgM-low anergic-like cells in Gal9KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J,K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J,K

claim: Higher titers of HEL-specific antibodies are detected in the serum of Gal9KO MD4/ML5 mice compared to MD4/ML5 WT controls.
source: Additionally, we detect higher titers of HEL-specific antibodies in the serum of Gal9KO MD4/ML5 mice compared to MD4/ML5 WT controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L

claim: There is a breakdown in peripheral tolerance in the absence of Gal9, leading to a population of cells that escape tolerance mechanisms.
source: These data suggest there is a breakdown in peripheral tolerance in the absence of Gal9, leading to a population of cells that escape tolerance mechanisms.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: B-1a cells are a population of B cells derived from fetal progenitors that undergo a positive selection process during development.
source: B-1a cells are a population of B cells derived from fetal progenitors that undergo a positive selection process during development, providing B-1a cells with an autoreactive repertoire.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about B-1a cells

claim: B-1a cells have an autoreactive repertoire.
source: B-1a cells are a population of B cells derived from fetal progenitors that undergo a positive selection process during development, providing B-1a cells with an autoreactive repertoire.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about B-1a cells

claim: B-1a cells are defined by their expression of the T cell regulatory protein CD5.
source: B-1a cells, defined by their expression of the T cell regulatory protein CD5, along with CD5-negative B-1b cells are typically found at barrier sites such as the lining of the gastrointestinal tract and peritoneal (PerC)/pleural cavities.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about B-1a cells

claim: B-1 cells rapidly respond to both BCR and TLR stimulation and can readily secrete antibodies in the absence of T cell help.
source: B-1 cells rapidly respond to both BCR and TLR stimulation and can readily secrete antibodies in the absence of T cell help.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about B-1 cells

claim: B-1a cells are expanded in several models of autoimmunity.
source: Intriguingly, B-1a cells are expanded in several models of autoimmunity, though their specific role remains incompletely defined (Duan and Morel, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Duan and Morel, 2006)

claim: There is an increase in the proportion of B-1a cells in the PerC of Gal9KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Indeed, we find an increase in the proportion of B-1a cells in the PerC of Gal9KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: There is an increase in cell number for B-1a cells in the PerC of Gal9KO mice.
source: Additionally, we see an increase in cell number for B-1a cells in the PerC of Gal9KO mice (data not shown).
evidence: Mentioned in text but data not shown

claim: B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice have higher expression of activation markers at steady-state.
source: Furthermore, B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice have higher expression of activation markers at steady-state (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting that Gal9 restrains B-1a activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: Gal9 restrains B-1a activation.
source: Furthermore, B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice have higher expression of activation markers at steady-state (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting that Gal9 restrains B-1a activation.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 4

claim: There is an expanded population of ASCs in the PerC of aged Gal9KO mice compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Consistent with our previous results, we find an expanded population of ASCs in the PerC of aged Gal9KO mice compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: Gal9KO mice have an increase in PC-specific antibodies.
source: We performed PC-specific ELISAs and found that Gal9KO mice have an increase in PC-specific antibodies, consistent with their increased ASCs (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: There is an expanded population of B-1a cells in the spleen of Gal9KO mice compared to WT littermates.
source: Consistent with this, we see an expanded population of B-1a cells in the spleen of Gal9KO mice compared to WT littermates (Figure 4H–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H–K

claim: There is an increase in B-1a cells in the thymus of aged Gal9KO mice.
source: Similarly, we see an increase in B-1a cells in the thymus of aged Gal9KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G

claim: Gal9 regulates B-1a cell accumulation and activation at steady-state.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates B-1a cell accumulation and activation at steady-state and implicate B-1a cells in the autoimmune phenotype observed in Gal9-deficient mice.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 4

claim: B-1a cells are implicated in the autoimmune phenotype observed in Gal9-deficient mice.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates B-1a cell accumulation and activation at steady-state and implicate B-1a cells in the autoimmune phenotype observed in Gal9-deficient mice.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 4

claim: Loss of Gal9 leads to enhanced activation of B-1a cells in response to lower concentrations of anti-IgM F(ab')2.
source: We find that loss of Gal9 leads to enhanced activation of B-1a cells in response to lower concentrations of agonist (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C

claim: Increased activation upon loss of Gal9 is specific to B-1a cells, as no difference was observed in B-1b cell responses.
source: Notably, this increased activation upon loss of Gal9 is specific to B-1a cells, as we did not observe any difference in B-1b cell responses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Gal9KO B-1a cells have enhanced phosphorylation of signaling machinery following IgM stimulation.
source: We see that Gal9KO B-1a cells have enhanced phosphorylation of signaling machinery following IgM stimulation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Pan-galectin inhibition in WT B cells results in increased signal transduction.
source: Following IgM stimulation, pan-galectin inhibition in WT B cells results in increased signal transduction and importantly, reconstitution of Gal9 in Gal9KO cells directly inhibits signaling in B-1a cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Reconstitution of Gal9 in Gal9KO cells directly inhibits signaling in B-1a cells.
source: Following IgM stimulation, pan-galectin inhibition in WT B cells results in increased signal transduction and importantly, reconstitution of Gal9 in Gal9KO cells directly inhibits signaling in B-1a cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Lactose and rGal9 treatments have little effect on B-1b cell signaling.
source: In contrast, but consistent with our earlier observations, these treatments have little effect on B-1b cell signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: B-1a cells have higher expression of Gal9 at steady-state compared to B-1b cells.
source: Indeed, B-1a cells have higher expression of Gal9 at steady-state compared to B-1b cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Gal9 has a specific role in the regulation of B-1a, but not B-1b cells.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate a specific role for Gal9 in the regulation of B-1a, but not B-1b cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5

claim: Gal9 interacts with IgM-BCR in B-1a, B-1b, and B-2 B cells.
source: We find that Gal9 interacts with IgM-BCR in B-1a, B-1b, and B-2 B cells, but uniquely interacts with the inhibitory glyco-protein CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: Gal9 uniquely interacts with the inhibitory glyco-protein CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells.
source: We find that Gal9 interacts with IgM-BCR in B-1a, B-1b, and B-2 B cells, but uniquely interacts with the inhibitory glyco-protein CD5 on the surface of B-1a cells (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: Gal9 binds to B-1a cells and regulates their activation, likely through the inhibitory co-receptor CD5.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 binds to B-1a cells and regulates their activation, likely through the inhibitory co-receptor CD5.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5

claim: IgM appears to be more clustered on B-1a cells in the absence of Gal9.
source: Upon visual inspection of dSTORM images, IgM appears to be more clustered on B-1a cells in the absence of Gal9 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of dSTORM images shown in Figure 5G

claim: IgM clusters are larger in the absence of Gal9 on B-1a cells.
source: Quantification of cluster area demonstrated that IgM clusters are larger in the absence of Gal9 (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H

claim: IgM on the surface of Gal9KO B-1a cells has a higher clustering tendency compared to WT B-1a cells.
source: We find that IgM on the surface of Gal9KO B-1a cells has a higher clustering tendency compared to WT B-1a cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I

claim: CD5 cluster area and degree of clustering are increased in Gal9KO B-1a cells.
source: However, quantification of CD5 cluster area and degree of clustering revealed an increase in Gal9KO B-1a cells (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J,K

claim: There is an increase in the segregation of IgM-BCR and CD5 in the absence of Gal9 on B-1a cells.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L

claim: The mean CBC value per cell decreases in Gal9KO B-1a cells.
source: This results in a decrease in the mean CBC value per cell (Figure 5M) and a corresponding increase in the mean nearest neighbor (NN; Figure 5N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M

claim: There is no difference in the organization of IgM on the surface of B-1b cells in the absence of Gal9.
source: In contrast, but consistent with the lack of effect of Gal9 deficiency on B-1b B cell activation, we find no difference in the organization of IgM on the surface of B-1b cells in the absence of Gal9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–G

claim: Gal9 regulates B-1a BCR signaling through a unique and specific mechanism.
source: Taken together, these findings identify a unique and specific mechanism of Gal9 regulation of B-1a BCR signaling.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5

claim: B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice are more sensitive to LPS and CpG stimulation, but not imiquimod or zymosan stimulation.
source: Interestingly, we find that B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice are more sensitive to LPS and CpG stimulation, but not imiquimod or zymosan stimulation (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–D

claim: Gal9 appears to be dispensable for TLR activation of B-1b cells.
source: In contrast, but consistent with BCR stimulation, Gal9 appears to be dispensable for TLR activation of B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: Gal9KO B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, have increased total tyrosine phosphorylation at 10 min post-LPS stimulation.
source: We find that Gal9KO B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, have increased total tyrosine phosphorylation at 10 min post-LPS stimulation, which can be reduced to levels comparable to WT cells by pre-treatment with rGal9 (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: Pre-treatment of WT B-1a, but not B-1b, cells with lactose enhanced total tyrosine phosphorylation upon LPS stimulation.
source: Similarly, pre-treatment of WT B-1a, but not B-1b, cells with lactose to displace galectins, enhanced total tyrosine phosphorylation upon LPS stimulation (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: Gal9 binds TLR4 and the inhibitory molecule CD180 on B-1 cells.
source: We find that Gal9 binds TLR4 and the inhibitory molecule CD180 on B-1 cells, and to a lesser extent on B-2 B cells (Figure 6F,G), consistent with previous mass spectrometry analysis of Gal9 ligands in B2 B cells (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F,G

claim: In the absence of Gal9, the mean cluster area and clustering tendency of TLR4 is decreased on B-1a cells.
source: In the absence of Gal9 the mean cluster area and clustering tendency of TLR4 is decreased on B-1a cells (Figure 6I–J), but interestingly, Gal9 has no affect on the organization of TLR4 in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I–J

claim: Gal9 has no effect on the organization of TLR4 in B-1b cells.
source: In the absence of Gal9 the mean cluster area and clustering tendency of TLR4 is decreased on B-1a cells (Figure 6I–J), but interestingly, Gal9 has no affect on the organization of TLR4 in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H

claim: The clustering tendency of CD180 is decreased in the absence of Gal9 in B-1a cells.
source: Similarly, the clustering tendency of CD180 is decreased in the absence of Gal9 in B-1a cells; however, the area of CD180 clusters is larger (Figure 6H,K–L), whereas deficiency of Gal9 has no effect on the organization of CD180 in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,I–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H,K–L

claim: The area of CD180 clusters is larger in the absence of Gal9 in B-1a cells.
source: Similarly, the clustering tendency of CD180 is decreased in the absence of Gal9 in B-1a cells; however, the area of CD180 clusters is larger (Figure 6H,K–L), whereas deficiency of Gal9 has no effect on the organization of CD180 in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,I–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H,K–L

claim: Deficiency of Gal9 has no effect on the organization of CD180 in B-1b cells.
source: Similarly, the clustering tendency of CD180 is decreased in the absence of Gal9 in B-1a cells; however, the area of CD180 clusters is larger (Figure 6H,K–L), whereas deficiency of Gal9 has no effect on the organization of CD180 in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,I–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,I–J

claim: The mean CBC value of TLR4 and CD180 is decreased in B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: The mean CBC value of TLR4 and CD180 is decreased, and mean nearest-neighbor increased, in B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 6M–O), however there is no difference in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K,M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6M–O

claim: There is no difference in the mean CBC value of TLR4 and CD180 in B-1b cells from Gal9KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: The mean CBC value of TLR4 and CD180 is decreased, and mean nearest-neighbor increased, in B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 6M–O), however there is no difference in B-1b cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K,M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1K,M

claim: Gal9 increases the association of TLR4 and CD180 specifically on the surface of B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, to modulate TLR4 signaling.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 increases the association of TLR4 and CD180, specifically on the surface of B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, to modulate TLR4 signaling.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice more readily adopt an ASC phenotype following stimulation with LPS and anti-IgM.
source: We find that B-1a cells from Gal9KO mice more readily adopt an ASC phenotype following stimulation, which results in more secreted antibody in the culture supernatant (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–D

claim: Following low-dose LPS injection, upregulation of CD86 is enhanced in Gal9-deficient B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells.
source: Following low-dose LPS injection, upregulation of CD86 is enhanced in Gal9-deficient B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: There is a greater fold increase in both PC-specific IgM and IgG in Gal9KO mice 24 hr post low-dose LPS injection.
source: Indeed, we find a greater fold increase in both PC-specific IgM and IgG in Gal9KO mice 24 hr post low-dose LPS injection (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: ICs formed following LPS injection are capable of capturing CFSE-labeled apoptotic bodies and recruiting them to SCS macrophages in the spleen.
source: We find that ICs formed following LPS injection are capable of capturing CFSE-labeled ApoB and recruiting them to SCS macrophages in the spleen (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E

claim: Following 2 weeks of antibody transfer, ICs are detected in circulation as well as in the spleens of mice receiving B-1a-derived antibodies in both WT and Gal9KO recipient mice.
source: Following 2 weeks of antibody transfer, we detect ICs in circulation as well as in the spleens of mice receiving B-1a-derived antibodies in both WT and Gal9KO recipient mice (Figure 7F–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–K

claim: Following transfer of B-1a-derived antibodies, GCs formed in the spleen and autoantibodies are detected in circulation.
source: Following transfer of B-1a-derived antibodies, GCs formed in the spleen and autoantibodies are detected in circulation (Figure 7L–O).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L–O

claim: Low levels of protein secretion into the urine are detected 4 weeks following final antibody transfer, suggesting that mice begin to develop nephritis.
source: Additionally, we detect low levels of protein secretion into the urine at this time point, suggesting that these mice begin to develop nephritis (Figure 7P).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7P

claim: Gal9KO mice develop a more exaggerated autoimmune response following transfer of B-1a-derived antibodies.
source: These observations are further exacerbated in Gal9KO mice, which have a reduced threshold for B cell activation, and subsequently develop a more exaggerated autoimmune response (Figure 7L–P).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L–P

claim: Gal9 regulates BCR-driven and unique TLR-driven B-1a responses by regulating the association of these receptors with negative co-receptors.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates BCR-driven and unique TLR-driven B-1a responses by regulating the association of these receptors with negative co-receptors, loss of which enhances B-1a-derived antibody production and consequently autoantigen delivery to splenic B cells to drive autoimmunity.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 7

claim: Loss of Gal9 enhances B-1a-derived antibody production and consequently autoantigen delivery to splenic B cells to drive autoimmunity.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates BCR-driven and unique TLR-driven B-1a responses by regulating the association of these receptors with negative co-receptors, loss of which enhances B-1a-derived antibody production and consequently autoantigen delivery to splenic B cells to drive autoimmunity.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 7

claim: Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice produce anti-dsDNA IgG antibodies earlier in life compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Indeed, we find that Gal9-deficient mice produce anti-dsDNA IgG antibodies earlier in life compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Mice lacking Gal9 develop accelerated proteinuria compared to WT controls in the NZB/W F1 model.
source: Furthermore, mice lacking Gal9 expression develop accelerated proteinuria compared to WT controls (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice have a larger population of splenic GC B cells early in disease progression compared to WT littermates.
source: Consistent with these observations, Gal9-deficient mice have a larger population of splenic GC B cells early in disease progression compared to WT littermates (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C,D

claim: There is an increase in the proportion of splenic ASCs in Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice early in disease onset.
source: We see a similar increase in the proportion of splenic ASCs in Gal9-deficient mice early in disease onset (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E,F

claim: ASCs in Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice skew toward B220− long-lived ASCs.
source: These ASCs skew toward B220− long-lived ASCs, and consistent with this, we see enhanced immune complexes in circulation in mice lacking Gal9 (Figure 8G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8G

claim: Enhanced immune complexes are detected in circulation in Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice.
source: These ASCs skew toward B220− long-lived ASCs, and consistent with this, we see enhanced immune complexes in circulation in mice lacking Gal9 (Figure 8G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8H

claim: NZB/W F1 mice deficient in Gal9 have a larger population of peritoneal B-1a cells.
source: Indeed, NZB/W F1 mice deficient in Gal9 have a larger population of peritoneal B-1a cells (Figure 8I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8I

claim: There is an increased proportion of B-1 cells in the spleen in Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice.
source: Indeed, there is an increased proportion of B-1 cells in the spleen in Gal9-deficient mice (Figure 8J), and this population is enriched for B-1a cells (Figure 8K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8J

claim: The splenic B-1 cell population is enriched for B-1a cells in Gal9-deficient NZB/W F1 mice.
source: Indeed, there is an increased proportion of B-1 cells in the spleen in Gal9-deficient mice (Figure 8J), and this population is enriched for B-1a cells (Figure 8K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8K

claim: Loss of Gal9 leads to enhanced production of B-1a-derived PC-specific IgM antibodies detectable in the serum of NZB/W F1 mice.
source: Furthermore, loss of Gal9 leads to enhanced production of B-1a-derived PC-specific IgM antibodies detectable in the serum (Figure 8L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8L

claim: Gal9 regulates the onset and progression of lupus-like disease in mice.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that Gal9 regulates the onset and progression of lupus-like disease in mice.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 8

claim: Loss of Gal9 leads to accelerated B cell-driven autoimmunity, marked by GC B cell and ASC formation as well as B-1a cell expansion, migration, and antibody secretion.
source: Loss of Gal9 leads to accelerated B cell-driven autoimmunity, marked by GC B cell and ASC formation as well as B-1a cell expansion, migration, and antibody secretion.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 8

claim: Gal9 modulates antigen affinity discrimination in B cells.
source: Our findings suggest that Gal9 modulates antigen affinity discrimination in B cells, a critical regulatory step in peripheral tolerance (Basten and Silveira, 2010).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and supported by citation (Basten and Silveira, 2010)

claim: Unchecked signal transduction leads to autoimmunity in mice.
source: Unchecked signal transduction leads to autoimmunity in mice (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017)

claim: Aberrations in CD19 or BTK signaling lead to autoantibody production.
source: In fact, aberrations in CD19 or BTK signaling, both of which are known to play important roles in defining this threshold of activation, lead to autoantibody production (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017)

claim: Negative regulators such as CD45 and CD22 play central roles in restraining B cell activation and are critical for antigen affinity discrimination in vivo.
source: Additionally, it is well established that negative regulators such as CD45 and CD22 play central roles in restraining B cell activation and are critical for antigen affinity discrimination in vivo (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zikherman and Lowell, 2017)

claim: By fine-tuning signal transduction networks, Gal9 coordinates affinity discrimination of B cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that by fine-tuning these signal transduction networks, Gal9 coordinates affinity discrimination of B cells and that loss of this regulation leads to the development of autoimmunity in mice.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Administration of rGal9 to NZB/W F1 mice prior to disease manifestation led to a reduction in disease severity.
source: For example, administration of rGal9 to NZB/W F1 mice prior to disease manifestation led to a reduction in disease severity (Panda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Panda et al., 2018)

claim: Gal9 restrains TLR7 and TLR9 responses in pDCs.
source: In this work, the authors elucidated a role for Gal9 in restraining TLR7 and TLR9 responses in pDCs, important drivers of type I IFNs and the inflammatory profile that supports autoimmunity (Panda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Panda et al., 2018)

claim: Gal9 regulates TLR4 and TLR9 responses specifically in B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells.
source: Mechanistically, we show that Gal9 regulates TLR4 and TLR9 responses specifically in B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, although unlike in pDCs, we see no effect of Gal9 on TLR7 responses in B-1 cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: Gal9 has no effect on TLR7 responses in B-1 cells.
source: Mechanistically, we show that Gal9 regulates TLR4 and TLR9 responses specifically in B-1a cells, but not B-1b cells, although unlike in pDCs, we see no effect of Gal9 on TLR7 responses in B-1 cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: Gal9KO mice have significantly reduced disease severity in the pristane-induced model of autoimmunity.
source: For example, Gal9 seems to be essential for development of autoimmune disease in the pristane-induced model, where Gal9KO mice have significantly reduced disease severity (Moritoki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Moritoki et al., 2013)

claim: Intracellular Gal9 interacts with the cortical actin cytoskeleton to facilitate phagocytosis and DC activation.
source: In this case, intracellular Gal9 interacts with the cortical actin cytoskeleton to facilitate phagocytosis and DC activation (Querol Cano et al., 2019), and therefore, genetic deletion of Gal9 may be detrimental for DC-dependent models of autoimmunity.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Querol Cano et al., 2019)

claim: Transfer of apoptotic bodies into mice is sufficient to drive autoantibody production.
source: Transfer of apoptotic bodies into mice is sufficient to drive autoantibody production, likely through increasing the density of autoantigens in secondary lymphoid organs (Mevorach et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Mevorach et al., 1998)

claim: Mutations that impair efferocytosis of circulating immune complexes can lead to autoimmunity.
source: Similarly, mutations that impair efferocytosis of circulating immune complexes can lead to autoimmunity (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018)

claim: Enhanced production of B-1a-derived antibodies increases circulating immune complexes in mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that enhanced production of B-1a-derived antibodies increases circulating immune complexes in mice and that these immune complexes transit to secondary lymphoid organs and are captured by SCS macrophages.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 7

claim: Immune complexes transit to secondary lymphoid organs and are captured by SCS macrophages.
source: Here, we demonstrate that enhanced production of B-1a-derived antibodies increases circulating immune complexes in mice and that these immune complexes transit to secondary lymphoid organs and are captured by SCS macrophages.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 7

claim: Expression of Gal9 is altered in a variety of disease conditions, including viral infection, inflammation, and cancer.
source: There is ample evidence that expression of Gal9 is altered in a variety of disease conditions, including viral infection, inflammation, and cancer (Chagan-Yasutan et al., 2013; Chou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Chagan-Yasutan et al., 2013; Chou et al., 2018)

claim: Gal9 is elevated in the serum in the context of autoimmunity.
source: In the context of autoimmunity, emerging evidence has suggested that Gal9 is elevated in the serum (Matsuoka et al., 2020); however, these results should be interpreted with caution, as degraded Gal9 in the serum could obscure the interpretation of these findings (Robinson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Matsuoka et al., 2020; Robinson et al., 2019)

claim: Upregulation of the I-branching enzyme GCNT2 in GC B cells leads to a concomitant decrease in Gal9 binding.
source: Indeed, selective glycosyltransferase expression may be a mechanism to disparately regulate that activity of galectin binding in B cells, as recent work has demonstrated upregulation of the I-branching enzyme GCNT2 in GC B cells, but not naïve and memory B cells, with a concomitant decrease in Gal9 binding (Giovannone et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Giovannone et al., 2018)
